subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: PCR Basics — Steps, Reagents and Controls

subjective.topic: PCR Basics — Steps, Reagents and Controls
subjective.question: Differentiate between the three steps of PCR (denaturation, annealing and extension).
subjective.answer: Denaturation: It is the first regular cycling event and consists of heating the reaction to 93°C–98°C for 20–45 seconds. It causes melting of the DNA template, yielding single strands of DNA. Annealing: The reaction temperature is lowered to 40–65°C for 20–40 seconds, allowing annealing of the primers to the single-stranded DNA template. Extension: The temperature at this step depends on the type of DNA polymerase used. Taq polymerase has its optimum activity temperature at 70–80°C; commonly 72°C is used. At this step the DNA polymerase synthesizes a new DNA strand complementary to the DNA template strand by adding dNTPs.

subjective.topic: PCR Basics — Steps, Reagents and Controls
subjective.question: Describe the denaturation step of PCR.
subjective.answer: Denaturation is the first regular cycling event and consists of heating the reaction to 93°C–98°C for 20–45 seconds. It causes melting of the DNA template, yielding single strands of DNA. The denaturation temperature reduces double-stranded molecules to single-stranded molecules (90–96°C, 20–45 seconds).

subjective.topic: PCR Basics — Steps, Reagents and Controls
subjective.question: What chemical reagents are used in conventional (standard) PCR? Give the reason why they are used. (3–5 Marks)
subjective.answer: A complete polymerase chain reaction (PCR) requires the following reagents: • DNA template — the DNA to be amplified. • Forward and reverse primers — short single-stranded DNA fragments (18–30 bp) that anneal to the template and start synthesis. • DNA polymerase (e.g. Taq polymerase) — the enzyme that synthesizes the new DNA strand. • Deoxynucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs) — the building blocks from which the new strand is made. • Reaction buffer and MgCl2 — provide the suitable conditions (including magnesium ions) for the polymerase to work. • Distilled water — to make up the reaction volume.

subjective.topic: PCR Basics — Steps, Reagents and Controls
subjective.question: What is a negative control? Differentiate between a negative control and a blank reaction.
subjective.answer: Negative control: It controls for the specificity of the amplification reaction. It contains all the reagents and a DNA template lacking the target sequence (so no specific product should be amplified). Blank reaction: It controls for contamination. It contains all the reagents except the DNA template.

subjective.topic: PCR Basics — Steps, Reagents and Controls
subjective.question: What are dNTPs?
subjective.answer: Deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) are the building blocks from which the DNA polymerase synthesizes a new DNA strand during successive cycles of PCR amplification. dNTPs consist of four basic nucleotides — dATP, dCTP, dGTP and dTTP. The concentration of each dNTP in the PCR is usually 200 μM.

subjective.topic: PCR Basics — Steps, Reagents and Controls
subjective.question: What are the advantages of PCR?
subjective.answer: PCR is: (1) specific, (2) simple, rapid and relatively inexpensive, (3) it amplifies from low quantities of DNA, (4) it works on damaged DNA, (5) it is sensitive, and (6) it is flexible.

subjective.topic: PCR Basics — Steps, Reagents and Controls
subjective.question: What are the limitations of PCR?
subjective.answer: The limitations of PCR are: (1) contamination risk, (2) primer complexities, (3) primer-binding site complexities, (4) it amplifies rare species, and (5) the detection method.

subjective.topic: PCR Basics — Steps, Reagents and Controls
subjective.question: Write the main steps (rules) for designing primers for PCR.
subjective.answer: • Keep the melting temperatures (Tm) of each primer pair within 2°C of one another. • Use an annealing temperature (Ta) 3–5°C below the melting temperature. • Keep primers between 18–22 base pairs long. • Design primers with a GC content of 35–65%.

subjective.question: Differentiate between Nested PCR and Multiplex PCR.
subjective.answer: Nested PCR: Two pairs (instead of one pair) of PCR primers are used to amplify a fragment. The first pair amplifies a fragment similar to standard PCR, and the second pair (the nested primers, which lie within the first fragment) amplifies a smaller fragment inside it. It has a very low probability of nonspecific amplification. Multiplex PCR: It is a variant of PCR which enables the simultaneous amplification of many targets of interest in one reaction by using more than one pair of primers. Multiple, unique primer sets are used within a single PCR reaction to produce amplicons of varying sizes specific to different DNA sequences.

subjective.question: What is In Situ PCR?
subjective.answer: In Situ PCR (ISH) is a polymerase chain reaction that actually takes place inside the cell on a slide. In situ PCR amplification can be performed on fixed tissue or cells. It applies the methodology of hybridization of the nucleic acids, allows identification of cellular markers, and is limited to detection of non-genomic material such as RNA.

subjective.question: What is Asymmetric PCR? What are its uses?
subjective.answer: Asymmetric PCR is used to amplify one strand of the original DNA more than the other. PCR is carried out as usual, but with a great excess of one primer for the chosen strand; due to the slow amplification later in the reaction after the limiting primer has been used up, extra cycles of PCR are required. Uses: It finds use in some types of sequencing and hybridization probing, where having only one of the two complementary strands is required.

subjective.question: Differentiate between Colony PCR, In Situ PCR and Asymmetric PCR.
subjective.answer: Colony PCR: It is the screening of bacterial or yeast clones for correct ligation or plasmid products. In Situ PCR: It is a polymerase chain reaction that actually takes place inside the cell on a slide; amplification can be performed on fixed tissue or cells. Asymmetric PCR: It is used to amplify one strand of the original DNA more than the other, and is used in some types of sequencing and hybridization probing where having only one of the two complementary strands is ideal.

subjective.question: What is Hot Start PCR?
subjective.answer: Hot Start PCR is a technique that reduces nonspecific amplification during the initial set-up stages of the PCR. The technique may be performed manually by heating the reaction components up to the melting temperature (e.g. 95°C) before adding the polymerase. Specialized enzyme systems have also been developed that inhibit the polymerase's activity at ambient temperature, either by the binding of an antibody or by the presence of covalently bound inhibitors that only dissociate after a high-temperature activation step. Thermophilic DNA polymerases (eubacterial type I DNA polymerase, Pfu) show very small polymerase activity at room temperature.

subjective.question: What is Mini Primer PCR (mini-primers)?
subjective.answer: Mini Primer PCR uses a thermostable polymerase (S-Tbr) that can extend from short primers as short as 9 or 10 nucleotides. This method permits PCR targeting to smaller primer binding regions, and is used to amplify conserved DNA sequences, such as the 16S (or eukaryotic 18S) rRNA gene.

subjective.question: What is Assembly PCR? Give its principle and methodology.
subjective.answer: Assembly PCR is the synthesis of long DNA structures by performing PCR on a pool of long oligonucleotides with short overlapping segments. It is used to assemble two or more pieces of DNA into one piece. Methodology: It involves an initial PCR with primers that have an overlap, and a second PCR using the products as the template, which generates the final full-length product.

subjective.question: What is Ligation Mediated PCR? Give its steps/principle and uses.
subjective.answer: Ligation Mediated PCR uses small DNA oligonucleotide 'linkers' (or adaptors) that are first ligated to fragments of the target DNA. PCR primers that anneal to the linker sequences are then used to amplify the target fragments. Uses: DNA sequencing, genome walking and DNA footprinting.

subjective.question: What is Methylation-Specific PCR (MSP)? What is the use of methylation in PCR?
subjective.answer: Methylation-specific PCR is used to identify patterns of DNA methylation at CpG islands in genomic DNA. Target DNA is first treated with sodium bisulfite, which converts unmethylated cytosine bases to uracil, which is complementary to adenosine in PCR primers. Two amplifications are then carried out on the bisulfite-treated DNA: one primer set anneals to DNA with cytosines (corresponding to methylated cytosine), and the other set anneals to DNA with uracil (corresponding to unmethylated cytosine). MSP used in quantitative PCR provides information about the methylation state of a given CpG island.

subjective.question: What is the WGA technique?
subjective.answer: Whole Genome Amplification (WGA) is a method for the robust amplification of an entire genome, starting with nanogram quantities of DNA and resulting in microgram quantities of amplified products. WGA has become an invaluable method for preserving limited samples of precious stock material, particularly when using WGA methods that have been developed to amplify material from a single cell.

subjective.question: What is Alu-PCR?
subjective.answer: The use of primers from a commonly repeated segment is called Alu-PCR, and it can help to amplify sequences adjacent to (or between) these repeats.

subjective.question: What is Real Time PCR (qPCR)? Give its methodology and ingredients.
subjective.answer: Real Time PCR is a technique in which fluorophores bind to specific target regions of amplicons to produce fluorescence during PCR. It is used to measure the quantity of a PCR product. The fluorescence, measured in real time, is detected in a PCR cycler with an inbuilt fluorometer, and it is the method of choice to quantitatively measure starting amounts of DNA, cDNA or RNA. Methodology/ingredients: QRT-PCR methods use fluorescent dyes, such as SYBR Green, or fluorophore-containing DNA probes, such as TaqMan, to measure the amount of amplified product in real time. Q-PCR is commonly used to determine whether a DNA sequence is present in a sample and the number of its copies in the sample.

subjective.question: Write the first step of RT-PCR.
subjective.answer: The first step of RT-PCR is the first strand reaction: synthesis of cDNA using oligo dT primers (37°C, one hour). This is followed by the second strand reaction — digestion of the cDNA:RNA hybrid (by RNase H) — and then standard PCR with DNA oligo primers.

subjective.question: How is the template different in RT-PCR from conventional PCR?
subjective.answer: In conventional PCR the template is DNA, while in RT-PCR the template we use is RNA (which is first converted into cDNA by reverse transcriptase).

subjective.question: Differentiate the methodology and principles of Allele-Specific PCR and AFLP PCR.
subjective.answer: AFLP PCR — Methodology: Genomic DNA is digested with one or more restriction enzymes, a tetracutter (MseI) and a hexacutter (EcoRI). Linkers are ligated to all restriction fragments. Pre-selective PCR is performed using primers which match the linkers and restriction-site-specific sequences. The amplicons are then separated electrophoretically on a gel matrix and the band pattern is visualized. AFLP is a highly sensitive PCR-based method for detecting polymorphisms in DNA, and it can also be used for genotyping individuals for a large number of loci. Allele-Specific PCR: It is used for identifying SNPs. It requires prior knowledge of a DNA sequence, including the differences between alleles, and uses primers whose 3' ends encompass the SNP. PCR amplification under stringent conditions is much less efficient in the presence of a mismatch between template and primer. This diagnostic or cloning technique is used to identify or utilize single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).

subjective.question: What does RAPD stand for?
subjective.answer: RAPD stands for Random Amplified Polymorphic DNA. It is a PCR-based technique in which a single short primer of arbitrary sequence is used to amplify random segments of genomic DNA, producing a pattern of bands (a fingerprint) that reveals polymorphisms between individuals.

subjective.question: Write the extension rates and sources of Taq, Vent and Pfu polymerases.
subjective.answer: Taq polymerase: extension rate 75 nucleotides/second; source — Thermus aquaticus. Vent polymerase: extension rate >80 nucleotides/second; source — Thermococcus litoralis. Pfu polymerase: extension rate 60 nucleotides/second; source — Pyrococcus furiosus.

subjective.question: Describe the types of Restriction and Modification (R-M) systems.
subjective.answer: At least four R-M systems are known: Type I, Type II, Type III and Type IIs. Type I: Type I systems were the first to be characterized, from E. coli K12. The active enzyme consists of two restriction subunits, two modification subunits and one recognition subunit. Type I systems are of little value for gene manipulation. Type II: Most of the useful R-M systems are Type II. Type II enzymes recognize a defined sequence and cut within it. Type III: Type III enzymes have symmetrical recognition sequences but otherwise resemble Type I systems, and are of little value. Type IIs: Type IIs systems have similar cofactors and structure to Type II, but restriction occurs at a distance from the recognition site, which limits their usefulness.

subjective.question: Give the nomenclature of restriction enzymes proposed by Smith and Nathans (1973).
subjective.answer: A suitable system of nomenclature was proposed by Smith and Nathans (1973). The species name of the host organism is identified by the first letter of the genus and the first two letters of the specific epithet: E. coli = Eco; H. influenzae = Hin. Strain identification is written after this, e.g. Eco K. In case the host strain has several restriction and modification systems, these are identified by Roman numerals, e.g. in H. influenzae: HindI, HindII.

subjective.question: On what do the number and size of restriction fragments depend? Give the expected spacing of 4-base, 6-base and 8-base recognition sites.
subjective.answer: The number and size of fragments generated by a restriction enzyme depend on the frequency of occurrence of the target site in the DNA to be cut. A four-base recognition site occurs every 4^4 (256) bp; a six-base recognition site occurs every 4^6 (4096) bp; and an eight-base recognition site occurs every 4^8 (65,536) bp.

subjective.question: What are the applications of PCR in microbiology?
subjective.answer: • Identification of bacteria. • Identification of slow-growing bacteria. • Detection of bacterial antibiotic resistance genes. • Viruses: identification of almost all viruses and measurement of viral load. • Fungi, e.g. Aspergillus spp. and Candida spp. • Parasites, e.g. Plasmodium spp. and Trypanosoma spp.

subjective.question: What are the forensic and other applications of PCR?
subjective.answer: • Forensic applications: DNA fingerprinting. • Detection of mutations: inherited disorders and carriers; tracking DNA abnormalities. • Prenatal diagnosis of genetic disorders. • Detection of pathogens. • Drug discovery. • Classification of organisms and genotyping. • Gene therapy and mutation screening.
